title: 26 U.S.C. 101 (certain death benefits: life insurance proceeds, transfer for value, employer-owned contracts)
publisher: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives (uscode.house.gov)
claims: Section 101(a)(1) provides that, except as otherwise provided in paragraphs (2) and (3), subsection (d), subsection (f), and subsection (j), gross income does not include amounts received under a life insurance contract, whether in a single sum or otherwise, if such amounts are paid by reason of the death of the insured.

Section 101(a)(2) provides that, in the case of a transfer for a valuable consideration, by assignment or otherwise, of a life insurance contract or any interest therein, the amount excluded from gross income by paragraph (1) shall not exceed the sum of the actual value of the consideration and the premiums and other amounts subsequently paid by the transferee.

Section 101(a)(2) provides that the transfer for value limitation does not apply to a transfer where the contract or interest has a basis in the hands of the transferee determined in whole or in part by reference to its basis in the hands of the transferor.

Section 101(a)(2) provides that the transfer for value limitation does not apply to a transfer to the insured, to a partner of the insured, to a partnership in which the insured is a partner, or to a corporation in which the insured is a shareholder or officer.

Section 101(a)(3) provides that the exceptions in the second sentence of paragraph (2) do not apply to a transfer of a life insurance contract, or any interest therein, which is a reportable policy sale.

Section 101(a)(3)(B) defines a reportable policy sale as the acquisition of an interest in a life insurance contract, directly or indirectly, if the acquirer has no substantial family, business, or financial relationship with the insured apart from the acquirer's interest in the contract, and provides that indirectly applies to the acquisition of an interest in a partnership, trust, or other entity that holds an interest in the contract.

Section 101(j)(1) provides that, in the case of an employer-owned life insurance contract, the amount excluded from the gross income of an applicable policyholder by reason of subsection (a)(1) shall not exceed the sum of the premiums and other amounts paid by the policyholder for the contract.
Section 101(j)(2) provides that paragraph (1) does not apply to the amounts it lists only in the case of a contract with respect to which the notice and consent requirements of paragraph (4) are met.

Section 101(j)(2)(A) lists amounts received by reason of the death of an insured who was an employee at any time during the 12-month period before the insured's death, or who, at the time the contract is issued, is a director, a highly compensated employee within the meaning of section 414(q) (without regard to paragraph (1)(B)(ii) thereof), or a highly compensated individual within the meaning of section 105(h)(5) with 35 percent substituted for 25 percent in subparagraph (C).

Section 101(j)(2)(B) lists amounts received by reason of the death of an insured to the extent the amount is paid to a member of the insured's family within the meaning of section 267(c)(4), to a designated beneficiary under the contract other than the applicable policyholder, to a trust established for the benefit of any such family member or designated beneficiary, or to the estate of the insured, or to the extent the amount is used to purchase an equity (or capital or profits) interest in the applicable policyholder from any such person.

Section 101(j)(3)(A) defines an employer-owned life insurance contract as a life insurance contract owned by a person engaged in a trade or business under which that person, or a related person, is directly or indirectly a beneficiary, and which covers the life of an insured who is an employee with respect to the trade or business of the applicable policyholder on the date the contract is issued.

Section 101(j)(3)(B) defines the applicable policyholder as the person engaged in a trade or business which owns the contract, and includes a person related to it under section 267(b) or 707(b)(1) or engaged in trades or businesses with it under common control within the meaning of section 52(a) or (b).

Section 101(j)(4) provides that the notice and consent requirements are met if, before the issuance of the contract, the employee is notified in writing that the applicable policyholder intends to insure the employee's life and of the maximum face amount for which the employee could be insured at the time the contract was issued, provides written consent to being insured under the contract and that such coverage may continue after the insured terminates employment, and is informed in writing that an applicable policyholder will be a beneficiary of any proceeds payable upon the death of the employee.

Section 101(j)(5) provides that employee includes an officer, director, and highly compensated employee within the meaning of section 414(q), and that insured means an individual covered by the contract who is a United States citizen or resident, with both individuals included in the case of a contract covering the joint lives of two individuals.

The Effective Date of 2006 Amendment note sets out section 863(d) of Pub. L. 109-280, which provides that the amendments apply to life insurance contracts issued after August 17, 2006, except a contract issued after that date pursuant to a section 1035 exchange for a contract issued on or before that date, and that any material increase in the death benefit or other material change causes the contract to be treated as a new contract.
updateCadence: Amended only by legislation. The official host showed the text in effect on September 29, 2026 at the time of access; the most recent amendment listed in the source credit is Pub. L. 115-97 (2017), whose note states it applies to transfers after December 31, 2017.
notes: Two features of this section are read past most often. Subsection (a)(2) is a limit on the exclusion that applies whenever a policy or an interest in it moves for value, and its exceptions are a closed list of named transferees, which subsection (a)(3) then switches off again for a reportable policy sale. Subsection (j) is a second limit that applies to employer-owned contracts, and its exceptions are available only where the written notice and consent in paragraph (4) were completed before the contract was issued. This record states what the text says. How either rule applies to a given arrangement is a question for a tax professional.
